parts.title: Using Sweden's Existing Wildlife Health Checks to Look for Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria in the Wild
parts.abstract:
ABSTRACT

Other researchers have already pointed out that we need to include wild animals when we check for antibiotic resistance, which is when bacteria can survive the medicines meant to kill them. In this study, we asked whether we could test Swedish wild animals for antibiotic resistance by using samples already collected by existing programs that check the health and disease of wildlife.

We studied six kinds of animals: bears, eagles, wolves, foxes, otters and hares. They sit at different levels of the food chain, and they come into contact with people to different degrees. We tested the samples for a common gut bacterium called Escherichia coli (E. coli). We looked for three kinds of E. coli that make enzymes able to break down antibiotics: ESBL-producing, pAmpC-producing and carbapenemase-producing. To find them, we grew bacteria on special growth plates that let only certain bacteria grow. From each sample we also grew one ordinary E. coli as a marker, which we call the indicator E. coli. We tested every E. coli we grew to see which antibiotics could still kill it. For some of them, we also read their full set of genes.

Two samples, both from foxes, carried ESBL- or pAmpC-producing E. coli. We found no carbapenemase-producing E. coli. Where the samples came from, together with the genetic details of the resistant bacteria, suggests that living near places shaped by people could play a part in whether wild animals carry antibiotic resistance. Our study also showed that using existing wildlife health checks is a low-cost way to keep watch for antibiotic resistance in wild animals. However, future studies and monitoring programs should think carefully about which animal species to choose and where they live.

Keywords: antibiotic resistance, tracing bacteria through genes and places, monitoring, wildlife
parts.introduction_first:
Wild animals that roam freely are never given antibiotics. Even so, many different kinds of wild animals carry antibiotic-resistant bacteria, which are bacteria that can survive the medicines meant to kill them (Allen et al. 2010; Laborda et al. 2022). Two things seem to affect how often this happens: how close an animal lives to places shaped by people, and what it eats. Wild animals that live near farm animals, feed on dead animals, or visit landfills and wastewater treatment plants carry these bacteria more often (Sharma et al. 2018; Ahlstrom et al. 2021; Woksepp et al. 2023; Höcketstaller et al. 2025). This points to a kind of pollution caused by people. It also raises a worry, because wild animals might build up these bacteria and then spread them to other places (Atterby et al. 2017; Lee et al. 2022).

Wild animals may also act as a storehouse for antibiotic-resistant bacteria. They may also be a place where new genes for antibiotic resistance appear (Guenther et al. 2011; Larsen et al. 2022). Researchers have described wild animals as a source from which disease-causing germs and antibiotic-resistant bacteria can enter the food chain (Greig et al. 2015). Some people who carry E. coli that makes ESBL enzymes, a type of enzyme that breaks down many penicillin-like antibiotics, have been linked to sources in the environment, including wildlife. However, there was little information about sources other than birds (Mughini-Gras et al. 2019). Researchers have also suggested that antibiotic resistance could pass along the food chain in nature, from one animal to the one that eats it (Jobbins and Alexander 2015).

Even so, we know very little about how often antibiotic-resistant bacteria turn up in top predators and in meat-eating animals that eat whatever they can find. These animals could build up resistant bacteria from their prey and from dead animals (Radhouani et al. 2014; Jobbins and Alexander 2015; Ramey and Ahlstrom 2020).
parts.introduction_rest:
Other researchers have already pointed out that we need to include wild animals when we check for antibiotic resistance (Saied 2024). However, setting up such programs can be complicated and expensive. For this reason, some have suggested using animals that are already part of existing programs that keep watch on wildlife (Doyle et al. 2025). Studies of wild birds have shown that these animals can act as sentinels, meaning early warning signs that antibiotic-resistant bacteria are present in the environment (Wyrsch et al. 2022; Woksepp et al. 2023; Nesporova et al. 2024). In contrast, there is still little research on land animals that come into contact with people in different ways.

In Sweden, several programs already exist to check the health and disease of wildlife (SVA 2023). On top of this, Sweden's Hunting Act says that if an animal from an endangered species, or from another species considered valuable, is found dead or killed, it should be handed over to the State (Jaktlag 1987: 259). Today, animals that count as 'state-owned wildlife' include, among others, bears, wolves, eagles and otters. The species listed in the official rules should be handed over to either the Swedish Museum of Natural History (SMNH) or the Swedish Veterinary Agency (SVA). The public is also encouraged to report and hand over to SVA any wild animals they find dead, sick or humanely killed. These existing programs and handovers give us a way to collect samples from wild animals for a program that checks for antibiotic-resistant bacteria, and they do so at low cost.

Having samples is only part of the problem. We also need a suitable marker, or indicator, to look for antibiotic-resistant bacteria. E. coli has been suggested as an indicator for checking the environment for antibiotic resistance, and it is already used in programs that check people and farm animals (Anjum et al. 2021). ESBL-producing E. coli is also used in the World Health Organization's (WHO) 'tricycle' protocol, a plan for checking antibiotic resistance across several areas at once (WHO 2021). E. coli is also found in most kinds of land animals, and ESBL-producing and carbapenemase-producing E. coli have been found in wild animals (Guenther et al. 2011; Dolejska and Literak 2019; Lagerstrom and Hadly 2021). So, learning how varied E. coli from wild animals are, both in their genes and in the antibiotics they can survive, could give us valuable information. That information would help us understand how antibiotic-resistant bacteria pass along the links between the environment, wild animals, farm animals and people.

In this study, we looked at how often we found ESBL-producing E. coli, pAmpC-producing E. coli, carbapenemase-producing E. coli and the indicator E. coli in samples collected as part of existing wildlife monitoring programs in Sweden. We also tested the E. coli we found, both by checking which antibiotics could still kill them and by reading their genes. The samples came from ongoing programs at SVA and SMNH that check the health and disease of wildlife. The animals we studied were brown bears (Ursus arctos), white-tailed and golden eagles (Haliaeetus albicilla and Aquila chrysaetos), Eurasian wolves (Canis lupus lupus), red foxes (Vulpes vulpes), European and mountain hares (Lepus europaeus and Lepus timidus), and Eurasian otters (Lutra lutra).

Our aim was to find out how often antibiotic-resistant bacteria occur in these wild animals, using a method similar to the one Sweden's programs for checking antibiotic resistance in food-producing animals already use (Folkhälsomyndigheten and SVA 2023). We also wanted to find out whether existing monitoring programs could be used in future programs that check for antibiotic resistance in wild animals.
parts.methods:
## 2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. Collecting the Samples

Between February 2020 and December 2023, we collected 358 samples of droppings (faeces) from six kinds of wild animals. The pathology department at SVA, the Swedish National Veterinary Institute, collected samples from brown bears (Ursus arctos), white-tailed eagles (Haliaeetus albicilla), golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos), Eurasian wolves (Canis lupus lupus), red foxes (Vulpes vulpes), European hares (Lepus europaeus) and mountain hares (Lepus timidus). These samples were taken during a necropsy, which is an examination of a dead animal's body (Table 1). The SMNH, the Swedish Museum of Natural History, collected the samples from Eurasian otters (Lutra lutra) (Table 1).

Brown bears, eagles, wolves and otters were sent to SVA and SMNH for necropsy because they were 'state owned wildlife'. Bears and wolves came mostly from protective hunting, where animals are hunted to protect farm animals. Most foxes were foxes that had been hunted and sent to SVA as part of a special monitoring program for the fox tapeworm (Echinococcus multilocularis) (SVA 2022). The hares were sent to SVA for general health checks of dead wildlife (SVA 2023).

When each dead animal arrived, we wrote down where it had come from. Most bodies were kept frozen at −20°C and thawed before the necropsy. How far the bodies had rotted varied, but we did not take samples from badly rotted ones.

TABLE 1

For each animal species: the number of samples we grew bacteria from, the number of samples that contained E. coli, the number of indicator E. coli that resisted at least one antibiotic, and the number of E. coli that made ESBL enzymes, pAmpC enzymes or carbapenemase enzymes.

| Animal | Number of samples | Number of samples with E. coli | Number of indicator E. coli resistant to at least one antibiotic | Number of ESBL- and pAmpC-producing E. coli | Number of carbapenemase-producing E. coli |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Brown bear | 108 | 86 (80%) | 3 | 0 | 0 |
| White-tailed eagle | 31 | 18 (58%) | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| Golden eagle | 4 | 2 (50%) | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| Eurasian wolf | 20 | 17 (85%) | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Red fox | 84 | 62 (74%) | 1 | 2 | 0 |
| European hare | 49 | 18 (37%) | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Mountain hare | 3 | 2 (67%) | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Eurasian otter | 59 | 8 (14%) | 0 | 0 | 0 |

We took the samples with FLOQSwabs eSwabs (Copan, Italy), which are swabs that carry a liquid for growing bacteria. We swabbed the bowel, the anal canal or the cloaca (the single opening at the rear of the body). We added 20% glycerol to the swabs and stored them at −80°C.

We also used the Statistics Sweden database, which we accessed in June 2025 (https://www.statistikdatabasen.scb.se/), to find out how many people lived in each county of Sweden in 2022.

### 2.2. Growing E. coli and the E. coli That Make ESBL, pAmpC and Carbapenemase Enzymes

We thawed the samples from brown bears and eagles. From each one, we moved 10 μL of the swab liquid into 2 mL of Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) broth (Oxoid Ltd., United Kingdom), a nutrient-rich liquid for growing bacteria. We added vancomycin at 8 mg/L to this broth. Vancomycin kills many other bacteria, so E. coli can grow more easily. We thawed the samples from wolves, red foxes, hares and otters and moved 10 μL of the swab liquid into 5 mL of buffer peptone water (Millipore, France), a simple liquid that also helps bacteria grow. We kept all samples at 37°C for 20 ± 2 hours, with air available, so that bacteria could multiply. This first step is called pre-enrichment.

Next, we spread 10 μL of each broth onto three special growth plates: CHROMagar Orientation, CHROMagar C3GR and CHROMagar mSuperCarba (CHROMagar, France). Each plate lets only certain bacteria grow, and each one shows E. coli in its own colour. We kept the plates at 37°C for 20 ± 2 hours. To check that our plates and methods worked, we also grew three known strains of bacteria: Escherichia coli ATCC25922, Klebsiella pneumoniae CCUG45421 and Escherichia coli NCTC13476.

From each sample and each plate, we picked one colony that looked like E. coli, following the maker's instructions. A colony is a small spot of bacteria that grows from a single cell. To confirm that it really was E. coli, we used a MALDI-TOF microflex instrument (Bruker, Germany) with the MBT Compass Library (Bruker, version 2022, RUO). This instrument identifies bacteria by the pattern of their molecules. We accepted the result when the instrument's score was 2.0 or higher, as the maker recommends.

### 2.3. Testing Which Antibiotics Still Work

We tested which antibiotics could still kill each E. coli using disk diffusion on Mueller-Hinton agar, a standard growth plate that we made in our own lab. In disk diffusion, small paper disks soaked in antibiotics are placed on a plate covered with bacteria. If the antibiotic works, a clear ring with no bacteria forms around the disk. We followed the rules of the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST). To decide whether a bacterium was resistant, we used EUCAST's cut-off values for Enterobacterales, the group of gut bacteria that includes E. coli, from version 11 of its rules.

We tested thirteen antibiotics (Oxoid Ltd., United Kingdom): ampicillin (10 μg), cefadroxil (30 μg), chloramphenicol (30 μg), ciprofloxacin (5 μg), gentamycin (10 μg), mecillinam (10 μg), meropenem (10 μg), nalidixic acid (30 μg), nitrofurantoin (100 μg), piperacillin/tazobactam (30/6 μg), trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (1.25/23.75 μg), tetracycline (30 μg) and trimethoprim (5 μg).

We also tested the E. coli from the C3GR plates with a second method, called double disk synergy testing (EUCAST). In this test, two disks are placed close together. One holds an antibiotic that is blocked by enzymes, and the other holds an antibiotic that the enzymes cannot break down. If the two work together, the bacteria are more likely to be killed. We paired amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (20/10 μg) with cefepime (30 μg), cefoxitin (30 μg), ceftazidime (10 μg) and cefotaxime (5 μg) (Oxoid Ltd., United Kingdom).

We chose some E. coli to have their full set of genes read. These were all the E. coli that resisted at least one antibiotic in our tests. We also picked a random group of E. coli that the antibiotics could still kill, up to 20 per animal species.

### 2.4. Reading the Full Set of Genes and Studying the Results

The E. coli were read at the Science for Life Laboratory Clinical Genomics Facility (Solna, Sweden) on a NovaSeq X machine (Illumina). The machine read each piece of DNA from both ends, 150 letters from each end (2 × 150 bp paired-end).

The machine produces millions of short pieces of DNA code, called reads. We first reduced the number of reads to 120×, meaning each letter of the genome was read about 120 times on average. We then used the program Trimmomatic 0.39 (Bolger et al. 2014) to cut off the Illumina adapters, which are short tags added during the lab work, and to remove low-quality parts. We checked the quality of the trimmed reads with FastQC 0.12.0 (Andrews 2010). Finally, we joined the trimmed reads from both ends into longer stretches using SPAdes Genome Assembler v. 4.0.0 (Bankevich et al. 2012), set to its mode for single bacteria.

To look for genes that give resistance to antibiotics, we used the program staramr (Bharat et al. 2022) with the ResFinder database (September 2024). We counted a match only when it was more than 90% identical and covered more than 95% of the gene. To find single-letter changes in genes that give resistance, we used AMRFinder (accessed June 2025) (Feldgarden et al. 2019). To look for virulence factors, which are features that help bacteria cause disease, we used the VirulenceFinder 2.0 database (Joensen et al. 2014) (accessed June 2025), set to E. coli. We counted a match only when it was 95% identical and covered 100% of the gene.

We uploaded the reads to EnteroBase (accessed June 2025) (https://enterobase.warwick.ac.uk/species/index/ecoli). EnteroBase is a large online collection of E. coli genomes. There we confirmed the species and found the phylogroup, which is one of the main family branches of E. coli. We also used two ways of sorting E. coli into types. The first, Achtman 7 gene multi-locus sequence typing (MLST), sorts them by seven genes. The second, core-genome multi-locus sequence typing (cgMLST), sorts them by many more genes that nearly all E. coli share. We also identified the serotype, which is based on the bacteria's outer coat, and the type of the fimH gene, which helps E. coli stick to surfaces (Zhou et al. 2020).

Some E. coli belong to a group called Escherichia cryptic clade V, which is very similar to the species Escherichia marmotae. For these, we calculated the average nucleotide identity (ANI), which is the average share of matching letters between two genomes. We did this with JSpeciesWS (https://jspecies.ribohost.com/jspeciesws/) (Richter et al. 2016), using the genome of Escherichia marmotae YF8 (GCA_029962465.1) as the reference.

We looked more closely at some E. coli to see how closely their genomes were related to others in EnteroBase (June 2025). These were the E. coli that made ESBL or pAmpC enzymes, the indicator E. coli that carried genes for resistance to antibiotics, the E. coli that carried stx genes (genes for toxins), and the E. coli that belonged to four types of extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC), which are E. coli that cause infections outside the gut. These four types are ST10, ST58, ST131 and ST648. We used the hierarchical clustering (HierCC) labels (Zhou et al. 2021), which group genomes by how similar they are. We also built minimum spanning trees, which are maps that link the most similar genomes with the fewest steps. We made these from cgMLST V1 and HierCC V1 in EnteroBase, using the program GrapeTree with the NINJA NJ method.
parts.results:
## 3. Results

### 3.1. Very Few ESBL- and pAmpC-Producing E. coli, and None Making Carbapenemase Enzymes, in Swedish Wild Animals

We tested 358 samples. Only two of them carried ESBL- or pAmpC-producing E. coli, and both came from red foxes. We found no carbapenemase-producing E. coli at all (Table 1).

We confirmed that the ESBL-producing bacteria carried two genes for ESBL enzymes, called blaCTX-M-15 and blaOXA-1. The pAmpC-producing bacteria carried a gene for a pAmpC enzyme, called blaDHA-1. The two bacteria were quite different from each other. They belonged to different phylogroups, which are large family branches of E. coli. They also had different sequence types (STs), which are smaller family labels, and different serotypes, which are types based on the bacteria's outer coat (Table 2). Both were multidrug resistant, meaning they resisted three or more different classes of antibiotics.

The ESBL-producing bacterium (R7b) carried several virulence-associated genes. These are genes that help bacteria cause disease. The pAmpC-producing bacterium (R8b) carried several virulence-associated genes linked to a type of E. coli called enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC), which sticks to the gut lining in clumps (Supporting Information 1).

Next, we compared the bacteria's genes with those of other E. coli using a method called cgMLST. It counts how many genes differ between two bacteria, and each difference is called an allele difference. The ESBL-producing bacterium (R7b, ST1193) grouped with several genomes from people, including some from blood and urine. It differed from them by no more than 10 alleles (HC10 4073) (Figure S1). The pAmpC-producing bacterium (R8b, ST200) grouped with genomes from people, with no more than 50 alleles apart (HC50 21668) (Figure S2).

### 3.2. Very Few Antibiotic-Resistant Indicator E. coli in Swedish Wild Animals

We grew 213 E. coli from the 358 samples, which is 59.5% of all samples (Table 1). Of these 213, 206 (96.7%) were fully susceptible, meaning every antibiotic we tested could still kill them (Table 1). The other 7 (2.3%) resisted at least one antibiotic (Tables 1 and 3).

Two of these resistant bacteria resisted ampicillin in lab tests. However, neither carried any acquired antibiotic resistance genes, which are genes bacteria pick up from outside, and neither had any changes in its main DNA. None of the bacteria from wolves or hares carried acquired antibiotic resistance genes. Supporting Information 3 gives the zone diameters and cut-off values for the indicator E. coli. A zone diameter is the clear ring around a test well where bacteria cannot grow, and the cut-off values are the sizes that count as resistance.

We also looked for changes in the pmrB gene. Two such changes, called E123D and Y358N, are linked to resistance to the antibiotic colistin. We found E123D in 29 of the bacteria whose genes we read, and Y358N in 46.

### 3.3. What the Antibiotic-Susceptible Indicator E. coli Were Like

We picked 92 fully susceptible indicator E. coli at random to have their genes read. They came from brown bears (17), eagles (15), wolves (15), foxes (18), hares (19) and otters (8).

The bacteria fell into six phylogroups (Figure 1). The most common was B1, with 45 bacteria (48.9% of the 92). Next came B2, with 29 (31.5%), and E, with 7 (7.6%). The rest were spread across phylogroups A (2 bacteria; 2.2%), D (3; 3.3%) and F (2; 2.2%). Four bacteria (4.3%) belonged to Escherichia clade V, a branch of a close relative of E. coli. We identified them as Escherichia marmotae using ANI, a measure of how alike two genomes are.

FIGURE 1

Phylogroups of the antibiotic-susceptible indicator E. coli, shown by the animal they came from.

We also sorted the bacteria by sequence type (ST), which showed that they were very varied. Bacteria from every animal species were spread across 81 sequence types. The most common were ST88, ST131, ST446 and ST2521, with three bacteria each (3%). The serotypes and the fimH types, which are types of a gene that helps E. coli stick to the gut, were also very varied (Supporting Information 4).

We then compared our bacteria with a large public collection of E. coli genomes called EnteroBase. Two bacteria, one in ST10 and one in ST648, did not group with any other bacteria there, even when we allowed up to 100 alleles apart (under the HierCC HC100 designations). The ST58 bacterium (R25a) grouped with genomes from poultry, pigs, cattle and people, with no more than 100 alleles apart (HC100 25133). The ST131 bacterium (V3a) grouped with genomes from people, with no more than 50 alleles apart (HC50 7090). It also grouped with the other two ST131 bacteria (H1537Ec and H4567Ec), and with genomes from people, the environment and animals, with no more than 100 alleles apart (HC100 58).

Two bacteria carrying antibiotic resistance genes, both in ST88 (1031a1Bj and R6a), grouped together. They also grouped with genomes from people, farm animals and wild animals, with no more than 100 alleles apart (HC100 30962) (Figure S3).

One bacterium from an otter carried the gene fosA7, which gives resistance to the antibiotic fosfomycin. We did not test for fosfomycin in our lab tests.

### 3.4. Finding E. coli That Make Shiga Toxins (STEC)

All the indicator E. coli carried virulence-associated genes, but in different numbers and with different jobs. Bacteria in phylogroups A and clade V (E. marmotae) usually carried only a few of these genes. Bacteria in phylogroups B2 and C carried many. Supporting Information 4 gives the details.

Two indicator E. coli carried genes for shiga toxins, which are poisons that can damage the gut (Table 4). One of them (1010a1Bj) also carried other virulence-associated genes linked to sticking to the gut and taking up iron. The other (V14a) carried other virulence-associated genes linked to sticking to the gut, making enterohaemolysin (a toxin that breaks open red blood cells), taking up iron, and resisting complement, a part of the body's defence system (Supporting Information 4). Neither carried eae genes, which help E. coli attach to the gut, or any genes or changes that give antibiotic resistance.

| Brown bear | 1010a1Bj | B1 | ST17448 | O‐:H49 | fimH1084 | stx1a |

Using cgMLST, the stx1a bacterium (1010a1Bj, ST17448) grouped with genomes from people, with no more than 50 alleles apart (HC50 1865). The stx2b bacterium (V14a, ST26) grouped with genomes from deer, with no more than 50 alleles apart (HC50 29641).

### 3.5. Where the Samples Came From, and How This Relates to How Many People Live Nearby

Most of the bacteria whose genes we read came from samples taken in areas where few people live (Figure 2). For nine bear samples, we did not know the municipality, so we show them for the county they came from. For five otter samples and one wolf sample, we did not know where the samples came from, so they are not shown in the figure. The ESBL-producing bacterium came from a sample from Stockholm. The pAmpC-producing bacterium came from a sample from Kungsbacka municipality in Halland County. Supporting Information 5 gives the origin of every sample that carried indicator E. coli.

FIGURE 2

Where the bacteria whose genes we read came from, and how many people live in each county. Colours show the animal species. The legend marks the ESBL-producing, pAmpC-producing, antibiotic-resistant bacteria and the stx+ bacteria (those carrying shiga toxin genes).
parts.discussion:
## 4. Discussion: What Our Results Mean

In this study, we found no carbapenemase-producing E. coli. However, two foxes carried E. coli that made ESBL enzymes or pAmpC enzymes. This is a sharp contrast with earlier studies in Sweden that looked at wild animals and the environment. In mallard ducks, 47% of samples carried ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, the wider family of gut bacteria that E. coli belongs to (Hessman et al. 2018). In gulls, up to 17% of samples carried ESBL-producing E. coli, and some samples also carried carbapenemase-producing E. coli (Wallensten et al. 2011; Atterby et al. 2017; Woksepp et al. 2023). In surface waters such as lakes and rivers, 27 of 98 samples carried E. coli that made ESBL or pAmpC enzymes (Egervärn et al. 2017).

Our foxes also carried these bacteria less often than people in Sweden do, where the figure is 4.7%. Our rate was lower than, or about the same as, the rate in healthy farm animals, which is 0%–3% (Ny et al. 2017; Folkhälsomyndigheten and SVA 2023, 2024). It was, however, similar to the rate found earlier in Swedish corvids, the crow family, which was 2%. Those researchers suggested that the bird carrying the ESBL-producing strain probably picked it up from the environment, and that this could be linked to many people and farm animals living in the area (Söderlund et al. 2019).

In our foxes, 2 of the 62 E. coli we grew (3.2%) made ESBL or pAmpC enzymes. This is similar to the 3.4% reported in Norway (Mo et al. 2018), but lower than the 11.5% reported in Northern Ireland and the 10.5% reported in Poland (O'Hagan et al. 2021; Osińska et al. 2022). Both the ESBL-producing and the pAmpC-producing bacteria in our study came from foxes living in areas with many people. This suggests that living close to places shaped by people could affect how often foxes carry antibiotic resistance.

Red foxes are generalists, meaning they can live in many kinds of places, and they adapt very well to cities (Walton et al. 2017). They also make use of food that people provide (Fletcher et al. 2025). Earlier studies have suggested that as more and more wild animals come to live near people, foxes may become more resistant (Osińska et al. 2022). This supports the idea that contact with people affects how often antibiotic resistance appears in wild animals. A similar link has been reported in Norway (Mo et al. 2018), where all the ESBL- and pAmpC-producing bacteria came from samples taken in towns and cities.

The genetic details of our two resistant bacteria further support the idea that contact with people plays a part in whether foxes carry antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Scientists sort E. coli into family groups called phylogroups, and into smaller groups called sequence types (STs). The ESBL-producing bacterium belonged to ST1193 (O75:H5 fimH64). It carried a large set of virulence-associated genes, which are genes that help bacteria cause disease (Supporting Information 1). These genes are linked with extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli, or ExPEC, which are E. coli that cause infections outside the gut (Bélanger et al. 2011). E. coli ST1193-O75:H5-H64 has been described as a multidrug-resistant ExPEC clone that is spreading around the world (Johnson et al. 2019; Pitout et al. 2022). Our bacterium carried the blaCTX-M-15 gene, which makes an ESBL enzyme. This gene has spread around the globe and has been found before in bacteria from patients and from the environment (Bonnevie et al. 2025; Edman-Wallér et al. 2025; Elmarghani et al. 2025).

The pAmpC-producing bacterium belonged to ST200. It was multidrug-resistant, meaning it could survive several different kinds of antibiotics, and it carried several virulence-associated genes linked with enterotoxigenic E. coli, or EAEC, a type of E. coli that causes stomach and gut illness (Van Nederveen and Melton-Celsa 2025). ST200 bacteria have been linked with EAEC illness before, in Spain and India (Llorente et al. 2023; Modgil et al. 2024). Both of our resistant bacteria also grouped with bacteria from people when we compared them (Figures S1 and S2).

Resistant indicator E. coli were uncommon in our animals. We confirmed resistance only in two bacteria from bears, two from eagles, one from a fox and one from an otter (Table 3). This differs from reports from other European countries (Pinto et al. 2010; Guenther et al. 2012; Radhouani et al. 2012; Simões et al. 2012; Mo et al. 2018). Still, antibiotic resistance is less common in Sweden than in other countries (EFSA and ECDC 2024), so we could expect Swedish animals to carry resistant E. coli less often. Also, many of the animals in our study came from areas with few people, so little contact between wild animals and towns could also explain the low rate. Similar results have been seen in parts of Europe with little human influence (Literak et al. 2010; Kozoderović et al. 2021; Homeier-Bachmann et al. 2022; Mengistu et al. 2022). Wolves and otters have been found to eat different things depending on whether they live in Northern or Southern Europe (Torres and Fonseca 2016; Ståhlberg et al. 2017), and this could affect how often wild animals in different regions carry antibiotic resistance. However, comparisons with earlier studies should be made carefully, because the methods used differ, and so does the number of samples tested from each animal species.

We also chose only one indicator bacterium per sample. This matches the standard way of testing in monitoring programs, but it might make the variety of bacteria in a sample look smaller than it really is.

The low level of resistance in otters and eagles surprised us. Otters are generalists and top predators in rivers and lakes (Loy et al. 2022), and eagles are top predators and scavengers that feed on dead animals. We may also have grown too few E. coli from these animals, which probably came from limits in how we collected samples. The bodies were frozen before we took samples, and the samples were frozen before we tested them, and this is known to affect how many E. coli we can recover (Masters et al. 2015). The bodies were also at different stages of decay when they thawed. In eagles, we took samples with swabs from the cloaca, the single opening birds use for droppings, urine and laying eggs. Cloacal swabs are known to give a less true picture of the gut bacteria than swabs from droppings (Videvall et al. 2018).

Seven of the bacteria we grew resisted more than one antibiotic. Three of them belonged to phylogroup B1, and three belonged to phylogroup C and ST88. The three ST88 bacteria carried antibiotic-resistance genes, several genes linked with ExPEC causing disease, and grouped with bacteria from people and many different animals in EnteroBase, a large online database of E. coli genomes (Figure S3). Bacteria in phylogroup C usually cause fewer ExPEC infections in people than bacteria in phylogroups B2 and D, but earlier studies have suggested that this group could be a storehouse for antibiotic resistance (Massot et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2023). One of the bacteria belonged to phylogroup F and carried a gene that gives resistance to the antibiotic trimethoprim, along with several virulence-associated genes. Although less common, infections outside the gut caused by phylogroup F bacteria have been reported (Lau et al. 2008; Guo et al. 2015; Wang et al. 2023).

Many of the indicator bacteria had changes, called mutations, in a gene named pmrB. These changes have been linked with resistance to the antibiotic colistin (Delannoy et al. 2017; Luo et al. 2017; Furlan et al. 2022). However, we did not test whether colistin could still kill these bacteria. Earlier work has shown that these mutations probably do not mean the bacteria are truly resistant, but instead depend on which phylogroup the bacteria belong to (Butters et al. 2024).

To fully understand how people might affect this, and to judge the possible risk to the health of people and farm animals, we need to understand how E. coli in wild animals are related to each other. The genetic background of different strains plays an important part in whether they carry antibiotic-resistance genes and virulence-associated genes (Clermont et al. 2019; Denamur et al. 2021; Petitjean et al. 2021). So we read the genes of a random selection of indicator E. coli that all the antibiotics we tested could still kill. These bacteria were very varied genetically, and there were no clear differences between animal species in which phylogroups or sequence types they belonged to.

The most common phylogroup was B1, which is also the phylogroup most often described in wild animals (Gordon and Cowling 2003; Tenaillon et al. 2010; Lagerstrom and Hadly 2023). Phylogroup B2, which causes a large share of ExPEC infections in people (Halaji et al. 2022; Micenková et al. 2016), also turned up in every animal species, and these bacteria usually carried many virulence-associated genes. However, this fairly large number of virulence-associated genes in phylogroup B2 is probably linked with these bacteria living harmlessly in the gut (Le Gall et al. 2007; Köhler and Dobrindt 2011).

Two of the B2 bacteria belonged to ST131, but only one grouped with bacteria from people in EnteroBase, including some from blood and urine. This bacterium carried several virulence-associated genes, which points to a possible link with people and with causing disease. However, it did not carry the fimH30 or fimH41 versions of a gene that are linked with the outbreak-causing ESBL-producing E. coli ST131 (Johnson et al. 2013; Price et al. 2013).

Four of the bacteria were identified again as Escherichia marmotae, a close relative of E. coli. They carried the astA gene, which makes a heat-stable toxin called EAST1 (Ménard and Dubreuil 2002). E. marmotae has recently drawn more attention in clinics, but it was first described as being common in wild marmots (Marmota himalayana) (Liu et al. 2015; Sivertsen et al. 2022). However, our bacteria lacked other genes linked with causing disease, and they carried fewer virulence-associated genes than the other phylogroups, which suggests they have little potential to cause disease.

Among the bacteria that all the antibiotics could still kill, two were identified as Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli, or STEC. These bacteria make toxins that can cause serious illness in people, and our two came from a bear and a wolf. As far as we know, this is the first report of STEC found in brown bears and Eurasian wolves. An earlier study found an STEC carrying the stx1 gene in a wild wolf (C. lupus italicus) in Italy, but did not study that bacterium further (Bertelloni et al. 2024). STEC are usually thought to live mainly in farm animals such as cattle and sheep, but they can also be found in many kinds of wild birds and mammals, especially deer (Espinosa et al. 2018). When we compared our bacteria with genomes in EnteroBase, the wolf bacterium grouped with bacteria from deer in several countries. This suggests that hunting or scavenging deer could be one way that meat-eating animals come into contact with STEC.

In general, STEC carrying the stx1a or stx2b genes cause a large share of STEC cases in people. However, they are rarely linked with major outbreaks or the most serious cases of illness, and they are seen as a lower risk to human health (FAO and WHO 2018). In Sweden, ST26 caused 19 cases of STEC infection in people between 2023 and 2025, while no cases caused by STEC ST17448 have been reported during the same years (Lina Thebo, The Public Health Agency of Sweden, personal communication).

Overall, our results show that antibiotic resistance is uncommon in Swedish wild animals. This reflects the limited effect of people on these animals, and the generally low level of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in farm animals and people in Sweden. The animals in our study, especially foxes, could act as sentinel species, meaning animals that we watch to keep track of problems in their surroundings. These animals live near people to different degrees, and they have already been shown to carry antibiotic-resistant bacteria in other European countries. Although we found little antibiotic resistance in otters and eagles, these species could also be used as sentinels, because they are closely tied to rivers and lakes, live near people, and are found all over the country.

Despite some limitations, our study shows that existing wildlife monitoring programs could be a low-cost way to keep watch for antibiotic resistance in wild animals and the environment. Our results show that future monitoring programs should think carefully about which animal species to include, because where the animals live, their habitat and their behaviour may strongly affect the results.
